text: Overused-word lists are the norm in public 'humanize' skills, e.g. a Tier 1 banned list of 18 words including delve, tapestry, pivotal, testament; such files embed the seeded tokens in the instruction file itself. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: Anthropic states Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6 are more responsive to the system prompt, so prompts written to reduce undertriggering may now overtrigger; the fix is to dial back aggressive language, e.g. replace 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...' with 'Use this tool when...'. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: Anthropic also advises removing over-prompting such as 'If in doubt, use [tool]', which causes overtriggering, and says Claude 4.6 models may overtrigger on anti-laziness instructions that earlier models needed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: Language models show structural priming: they reuse recently seen syntactic structures, including when prime and target share no lexical overlap, indicating abstract structural representations. (high confidence)

text: Hooks cannot directly modify assistant message text. Stop can only prevent stopping and continue the conversation, and last_assistant_message on Stop/SubagentStop is read-only input for analysis. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: A mechanistic study of 40,000 samples reports that explicitly naming a forbidden word can raise its generation probability; priming failure accounts for 87.5% of negative-constraint violations and override failure for 12.5%. (medium confidence)

text: The same study finds violation probability tracks the model's intrinsic 'semantic pressure' toward the token (p = sigmoid(-2.40 + 2.27*P0)), so the risk is highest for high-prior tics such as delve, which are exactly the ones people list. (low confidence)

text: Independent evidence that emotional or emphatic framing improves accuracy is mixed: a 2026 arXiv study tests emotional framing across GPT, Llama, Qwen3 and DeepSeek on GSM8K, BBH, MedQA and others, and secondary reporting cites contradictory politeness studies (e.g. a 2025 GPT-4o result where impolite prompts scored 84.8% vs 80.8% for very polite). Effect sizes were not verified from the paper text. (low confidence)

text: A workable lint design: scan instruction files for tokens on a tic list and classify each hit as ban-list entry, example text or incidental prose; flag examples and prose hits first, since they show the word as a model to copy rather than as a prohibition. This is inferred from the sources, not documented anywhere. (low confidence)

text: Practical mitigation for instruction files: write the instruction file in the plain style wanted in the output (prose, little markdown) and state the desired format positively, rather than only listing prohibitions. (low confidence)

text: EQ-Bench's Slop Score is a weighted composite (60% slop words, 25% not-X-but-Y patterns, 15% slop trigrams) computed against human baselines (wordfreq for words, a human essay/creative corpus for trigrams); it is not an AI-vs-human classifier and may underreport outside creative writing and essays. (medium confidence)

text: OpenAI's GPT-4.1 guide says all-caps or incentives like bribes or tips are generally unnecessary, recommends starting without them, and warns that existing prompts using them may make GPT-4.1 attend to them too strictly. It attributes this to GPT-4.1 following instructions more literally than predecessors. (medium confidence)

text: Two vendors independently converge on the same hygiene rule: with current literal, steerable models, drop emphatic markers by default and add them back only if a specific prompt needs them. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: Guidance is model-scoped: the Anthropic advice targets Opus 4.5/4.6 and later; the same emphatic wording may still be needed on weaker or older models, so a lint rule should be per-model, not universal. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: A Stop hook can act as a post-generation filter: it inspects the final response and blocks with a reason, forcing the model to revise before the user sees the result. (medium confidence)

text: A regex-only Stop hook produces false positives; combining the regex with a second condition (e.g. prior tool-call activity) removes most of them. (low confidence)

text: A Stop hook that re-blocks without checking stop_hook_active can loop indefinitely; one reported case ran about 50 minutes and consumed the session quota. A nag-once pattern (block the first violation, let an identical repeat pass) avoids it. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-03)
keywords: Instruction-file hygiene for LLM lexical tics: linting, mirroring, hook filtering

text: PostToolUse can replace a tool's output before the model sees it (updatedToolOutput), so filtering applies to tool results but not to the model's own prose. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

text: The Verbal Tic Index (VTI) combines TicRate (share of responses containing a tic), MATTR lexical diversity, a sycophancy score and phrase repetition rate with weights 0.3/0.2/0.3/0.2; the authors say other weights may reorder models, so it is a comparative summary, not an absolute measure. Use response-level tic share as a simple before/after rate. (medium confidence)
